description: Team from Kyiv Polytechnic University, we are creating text game about space mission. No experience, but we’re trying.
summary:
Orbital Architect is a real-time, cooperative web simulation game for designing space missions to Low Earth Orbit (LEO), the Moon, and Mars. Built for solo play or teams of up to four, it divides mission control into four specialized roles: Science Lead, Bus Engineer, Flight Engineer, and Comms Specialist.
Players collaboratively configure scientific payloads, spacecraft buses, solar arrays, batteries, launch vehicles, stabilization systems, and ground station networks while balancing strict physical and financial constraints—mass, power, orbital eclipse survival, data downlink capacity, failure risk, and budget. Room-seeded hardware variations prevent memorized templates, while cutting corners on radiation hardening, micrometeorite shielding, or redundancy triggers simulated in-flight anomalies across four mission phases: Launch, Transit, Orbit Insertion, and Orbital Operations.
Space mission design is often viewed as isolated calculations rather than a tightly coupled, collaborative trade-off process. Orbital Architect transforms authentic systems engineering into an accessible, interactive experience that demonstrates how every subsystem decision directly shapes scientific return and mission survival.
details:
Orbital Architect is a real-time cooperative web game where 1 to 4 players design, test, and launch space missions to Low Earth Orbit, Lunar Polar Orbit, and Mars Reconnaissance Orbit. When playing solo, you control all four engineering stations yourself; in multiplayer, up to four teammates split the roles and work together in a shared room.

Each role handles a specific part of the spacecraft while sharing the same budget, mass limit, and power grid. The Science Lead chooses the spacecraft bus (with 2, 3, or 4 slots) and scientific instruments like Synthetic Aperture Radar, a quantum gravity gradiometer, or a subsurface ice radar, combining compatible instruments for synergy bonuses. The Bus Engineer configures solar panels (silicon, triple-junction GaAs, or flexible roll-out arrays) and batteries (NiH2, Li-Ion, or solid-state) so the spacecraft survives orbital eclipses, and adds micrometeorite shielding or subsystem redundancy. The Flight Engineer selects the launch vehicle that sets the maximum payload mass, picks the attitude stabilization system (which directly improves science output), and can install cold-gas, hydrazine, or xenon ion thrusters to extend operational lifetime and multiply science points. The Comms Specialist sets up S-, X-, or Ka-band transceivers, onboard solid-state memory, lossless or FPGA data compression, Deep Space Network ground stations (0 to 3), and radiation-hardened or encrypted electronics.

Before launch, the engine checks eight coupled constraints in real time: budget, spacecraft mass and bus slots, data recording rate, daily Earth downlink and blackout memory buffer, power generation versus load, eclipse battery capacity, minimum required science, and overall failure risk. Once everything is in the green, the mission launches through a four-stage simulation covering launch, transit, orbit insertion, and orbital operations. The game generates a flight telemetry log, calculates a final score from 0 to 100 based purely on net science delivered, and benchmarks the mission against real NASA analogs like Landsat-9, LRO, and MRO.

What makes the project creative is how it prevents players from relying on memorized builds. Every room generates a deterministic seed that shifts hardware stats by roughly 8 to 12 percent across mass, power, cost, data rates, and science yield. Everyone in the room sees the exact same numbers, so teammates have to analyze the trade-offs fresh each run. In addition, skipping protective hardware exposes the spacecraft to environment-scaled hazards during flight, such as micrometeorite hits, cosmic radiation bit-flips, or command-link interference, which damage subsystems and reduce final science points.

In building the simulation, we accounted for real orbital factors including solar irradiance drop-off at Mars (0.43 compared to 1.0 at Earth and the Moon), continuous eclipse durations up to 2.2 hours in lunar polar orbit, an 85 percent usable battery capacity margin, and data buffering across communication blackouts. The goal of the project is to make systems engineering intuitive and accessible directly in a browser, showing how a single hardware choice impacts the rest of the spacecraft and encouraging real-time teamwork.

The application was built using TypeScript, React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, with Firebase Realtime Database handling live room synchronization, player presence, role assignments, and atomic configuration updates. Development and deployment were done with Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub, and Vercel.
